newsitem.title: TURKEY: TURKEY'S ISLAMISTS IN PARLIAMENTARY CHALLENGE.
newsitem.headline: TURKEY'S ISLAMISTS IN PARLIAMENTARY CHALLENGE.

text.p: Turkey's battered Islamist-led government faces a fresh parliamentary challenge to its rule on Tuesday with the protests of both ordinary civilians and stern generals ringing in its ears.
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's coalition looked set to win a vote by MPs on whether to hold a censure motion against it within a week.
But military dissent, backed by street protests, has brought Erbakan to his lowest ebb since he became the first Islamist to lead modern Turkey last year.

The military-dominated National Security Council warned Erbakan at the weekend to end a recent surge in religious activism they fear could pave the way to turning NATO member Turkey into an Islamist state.
The army, which frequently leads opinion polls as the country's most respected institution, has ousted three governments since 1960.

Several thousand anti-Islamist demonstrators took to the streets of Istanbul and demonstrators sounded car horns, blew whistles and banged on pots and pans on Monday night to show displeasure at the surge in religious activism.
City and town residents have been switching their house lights on and off at 9 p.m. every night, symbolically callingor light to be shed on a security scandal.
The protest, originally supposed to last only until the end of February, has grown and taken on an anti-Islamist hue.
"The action will continue until they accept secularism or go," said 51-year-old clerk Osman Canturk at a demonstration in an Ankara park.
Protesters took to the streets on both the Asian and European shores of the Bosphorus strait in Istanbul, witnesses said.
People marched along the city's main Istiklal Street whistling and clapping. An employee banged a pot against the wall of his kebab shop to add to the din.
Erbakan has been unruffled by both the extra-parliamentary opposition and efforts in the national assembly to topple him. He gave the censure vote short shrift on Monday.

"Let's have one every week so we can confirm that the government is getting stronger," he told a news conference. Opposition parties have failed in two recent ballots to force Erbakan's government to step down.
But political analysts say he ignores the generals at his peril.
The army has a free hand in the fight against Kurdish rebels in the mountainous southeast and plays a major role in Turkey's many disputes with neighbours Greece and Cyprus.
Young officers are taught to idolise Turkey's secularist founder Kemal Ataturk, himself a military man.
Coalition partner Tansu Ciller, a pro-Western secularist, has so far stuck by Erbakan.

"Secularism will continue in Turkey, we are the guarantee of that," she told reporters after a two-hour meeting with Erbakan. "This government will continue. In this government there will be nothing contrary to secularism," she said.
